title: The trumpet
hookLine: the trumpet is blown, and all rise (39:68)

cards: Some sounds end things. A final whistle. A school bell at three.
An alarm at six that ends the night whether you're ready or not. The Qur'an speaks of one sound that ends everything, and then starts it again.

In Surah az-Zumar, Pickthall's translation reads: "And the trumpet is blown, and all who are in the heavens and all who are in the earth swoon away, save him whom Allah willeth. Then it is blown a second time, and behold them standing waiting!"
Two blasts. One to end, one to raise.

teach.b: You heard the trumpet in An-Naba' on day 221; today, both blasts. The Arabic is as-sur, a horn. It sounds in more than one surah, in az-Zumar and again in Ya Sin, in a short, sudden line: and the trumpet is blown.
Tradition names the angel who blows it Israfil, though the Qur'an itself doesn't give the name.

teach.h: THE SWOON, SAVE WHOM ALLAH WILLS.
teach.b: The first blast brings a swoon over everyone in the heavens and the earth, except whoever Allah wills. Who those exceptions are, the verse leaves open, and commentators have answered in different ways.
Then the second blast, and people stand, waiting. How long between the two?

teach.h: FORTY WHAT? HE DECLINED TO SAY.
teach.b: A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Hurayrah, says: between the two blasts is forty. Someone asks him: forty days? He declines to say.
Forty months? He declines. Forty years?

He declines again. A companion of the Prophet, peace be upon him, who would not go past what he had said, and readers take that restraint as part of the teaching. Then Ya Sin gives the moment of waking.

teach.h: WHO HATH RAISED US FROM OUR SLEEP?
teach.b: When the trumpet is blown, people hurry from their graves to their Lord, and their first words, Pickthall again, are: "Woe upon us! Who hath raised us from our place of sleep?"

The grave, from the far side, felt like sleep. The answer comes straight back: this is what the Beneficent promised, and the messengers told the truth. So in Muslim teaching the trumpet is not only an ending.
It's the sound that means nobody was lost.

how: Muslims believe the trumpet will be blown at the end of the world and again at the resurrection; the verses that describe it are recited in prayer and in sermons about the Last Day.

o: the call to prayer sounded from a mosque five times a day
the angel's voice that wakes each soul in the grave alone
the horn blown twice on the Day: once to end, once to raise

p: all swoon, save whom Allah wills

s: the Qur'an names the angel who blows the trumpet
tradition names him Israfil; the Qur'an doesn't give the name.
asked whether the forty was days, months or years, Abu Hurayrah declined to say
each time he was asked, he declined.
in Ya Sin, those raised call the grave a place of sleep
"Who hath raised us from our place of sleep?"

games.q: you're Abu Hurayrah. you've said: between the two blasts is forty. someone asks: forty days? what do you say?
games.why: he declined three times: days, months, years. he would not go past what he had said.

practice: Sit low, or lie down, and let your body go heavy, as if you'd been asleep a long time, with the line from Ya Sin in mind: who hath raised us from our place of sleep?
Near the end, rise slowly, feet taking your weight, spine lifting, head coming up last; if standing is hard, simply lift your head.
Stand still for a few breaths, with the verse from az-Zumar if you pray, or just noticing what it feels like to get up.

wordCard.voice: The trumpet. As-sur, the horn blown twice, the Qur'an says: once to end, once to raise. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the horn, or trumpet, of the Last Day.

carryVoice: Your line: all will rise. Nobody lost, and everyone standing, waiting. Same time tomorrow.

sources.q: And the trumpet is blown, and all who are in the heavens and all who are in the earth swoon away, save him whom Allah willeth. Then it is blown a second time, and behold them standing waiting!
Woe upon us! Who hath raised us from our place of sleep?
